headline: A Vanilla JS Port Demystifies Physics-Based Geospatial Rendering
lede: A developer named Jean Timex has ported Takram's *three-geospatial* demo from React Three Fiber into plain JavaScript, then layered on volumetric cloud and atmosphere effects — making the library's most visually striking capabilities reachable without a React build pipeline. The underlying library, built by Tokyo design-engineering studio Takram, implements a rigorous physical model of Earth's sky and atmosphere directly in the browser. The result is a live demo that renders photorealistic aerial haze, clouds, and lighting over a 3-D globe in WebGL.
body:
**three-geospatial** is a modular monorepo of Three.js packages, each tackling a different layer of geospatial rendering: a core that handles coordinate math and GIS data, an atmosphere package built on *precomputed atmospheric scattering* (a technique that bakes the physics of light bouncing through air into lookup textures), and a clouds package for volumetric 3-D clouds. The library is designed to compose with established tools such as *3d-tiles-renderer* and the *astronomy-engine*, rather than replace them.

The project originated as a prototype for a Web GIS engine built by Eukarya, a Japanese geospatial software firm, under a SBIR (Small Business Innovation Research) grant from Japan's Cabinet Office. Takram contributed the rendering layer; that phase of the work concluded in March 2025. The library was subsequently open-sourced under an MIT licence and now has roughly 1,100 GitHub stars.

The original public demo was written for *React Three Fiber* (R3F), a React renderer that lets developers describe Three.js 3-D scenes as declarative JSX components. R3F is productive for complex React apps but adds overhead — a React dependency, a bundler, and JSX compilation — that many developers want to skip. Jean Timex's port strips that away, exposing how the same atmosphere and cloud effects can be wired up in ordinary JavaScript. The atmosphere package handles sky colour, aerial perspective (the bluish haze that makes distant objects look faint), sun and star positions, and scattered light on surfaces; the clouds package adds geometry-shaded volumetric clouds rendered in a separate rendering pass.

The library's WebGPU support is listed as work in progress, with a node-based shader architecture intended to replace the current chunk-based one. The upgrade promises faster generation of atmosphere look-up tables and more accurate large-scale lighting, though the new API will be incompatible with the current one. For now, both the original R3F demo and Jean Timex's Vanilla JS port run on WebGL, which any modern browser supports without flags.

concepts.definition: A rendering technique for realistic sky and haze, pioneered by Bruneton and Neyret, that pre-calculates how sunlight scatters through air molecules and aerosols into a set of lookup textures. At runtime, the GPU samples those textures instead of simulating the physics from scratch each frame, making physically accurate sky colour and aerial perspective practical in real-time applications.

A React renderer for the Three.js 3-D library. It lets developers write 3-D scenes as JSX component trees — declarative, composable, and reactive — rather than imperative JavaScript calls. The tradeoff is a mandatory React runtime and build toolchain; Vanilla JS Three.js avoids both.

3-D clouds rendered by ray-marching through a volume of signed-distance or noise-based density data rather than painting a flat texture on a billboard. The technique produces self-shadowing, interior glow, and parallax that planar sprites cannot replicate, at significantly higher GPU cost.

An OGC community standard for streaming massive 3-D geospatial datasets — buildings, terrain, point clouds — as a spatial hierarchy of tiles loaded on demand. Libraries such as 3d-tiles-renderer implement the client side of this protocol for Three.js, allowing city-scale scenes to render without loading everything at once.

Japan's Small/Startup Business Innovation Research programme, administered by the Cabinet Office, funds technology development contracts between government agencies and small businesses. It parallels the US SBIR model: government defines a need, startups bid to build it, ownership of the result stays with the contractor.

repos.summary: A monorepo of Three.js libraries for geospatial rendering, covering atmosphere, volumetric clouds, GIS core utilities, and post-processing effects. Built by Takram for a Japanese government-funded Web GIS project and open-sourced under MIT. Packages are in Beta/Alpha status and designed to compose with 3d-tiles-renderer and astronomy-engine rather than replace them.

Jean Timex's Vanilla JavaScript port of the three-geospatial R3F demo, with cloud and atmosphere visual effects added on top. Removes the React/R3F dependency so developers can use the atmospheric rendering directly in plain Three.js projects. Accompanied by a live demo hosted on GitHub Pages.
